societies.name: Detroit: Become Human (before the android revolution)
societies.society: United States before the android revolution
societies.description:
Android service work has displaced a substantial part of the human workforce, while the machines are still treated as property. The result is an uneven transition: automation is widespread, but human society has not adopted an equally widespread entitlement to its output. The guarantee score therefore leans toward weak protection, with uncertainty about policies the consulted material does not describe.

CyberLife supplies the android technology, while households and businesses use individual units. Control is concentrated enough to sit near the elite band, but it is not literally one company owning every productive asset; the range allows for more distributed human ownership. The in-game news reports 37.3% unemployment. That figure is stored separately because unemployment is measured against a labor force, not all human residents. It cannot be copied into the nonworking axis. This record describes an automation-driven disruption, not a completed abolition of employment.

scope.period: Detroit and the United States in November 2038, before a successful android uprising
scope.population: Humans in the android-disrupted United States economy, with Detroit as the depicted focus
exclusions: Free android polities after a successful ending
An assumption that all humans have already stopped working

guarantees.basis: Major displacement and social conflict are supported; a universal material entitlement is not established.

control.basis: CyberLife's platform and manufacture coexist with many human purchasers and users.

nonworking.basis: The reported 37.3% unemployment rate has a different denominator from all humans.

evidence.claim: Major displacement and social conflict are supported; a universal material entitlement is not established.
evidence.locator: See the named source read_scope and the entry's scoped period

evidence.claim: CyberLife's platform and manufacture coexist with many human purchasers and users.
evidence.locator: See the named source read_scope and the entry's scoped period

societies.name: Fallout (prewar Appalachia)
societies.description:
Hornwright's records show a corporate drive to remove human labor from mining and expand automation further. Machines such as the Motherlode give this more substance than a general claim that the future has robots. The owners aim to preserve output while reducing their dependence on workers, and opposition to that policy is treated as an obstacle to corporate and political plans.

This is a partial transition toward the concentrated-control, weak-guarantee region. The sources establish displacement and elite control much more clearly than any replacement entitlement for the displaced population. They also retain human staff and describe further automation as a goal, so the record must not say that all work was already automated. The country-wide candidate is narrowed here to the region actually supported by the evidence. The prewar notes and the postwar date when a player finds them are kept distinct. No population-wide nonworking figure is supplied.

scope.population: Humans in Appalachia's corporate mining and automation conflict
exclusions: All prewar America as a statistically uniform society

societies.name: Fallout 4 (The Institute)
societies.description:
The Institute uses synth labor to support an unusually well-provisioned enclave within the ruined Commonwealth. Its scientific divisions maintain food and health services, while ordinary synthetic workers perform many service and maintenance tasks. This supports an enclave-scale post-work comparison: a privileged human population benefits from manufactured labor while retaining scientific and managerial vocations.

Control is concentrated in the Directorate and its leadership. For born-human residents, material provision appears much stronger than it does outside, so the guarantee score is moderately protective. That is a deliberately narrow population choice. It does not grant the same security to synth persons or to surface communities, and a wider assessment would move toward weak guarantees. Because the laboring synths have contested personhood, the entry explicitly discloses whose leisure is being measured. The consulted material does not establish an unconditional right to remain supported regardless of role, or a percentage of nonworking humans.

scope.period: The Institute in 2287 before any branch destroys or replaces its leadership
scope.population: Born-human Institute residents; synth persons are explicitly treated as the excluded laboring population
exclusions: A guarantee to the Commonwealth's surface population
An assumption that synth labor is morally equivalent to an inert tool
All humans having stopped research and technical work

societies.name: Cyberpunk 2077 (Night City)
societies.description:
Night City has advanced machine intelligence and a sharp separation between protected wealth and exposed poverty. The game's North Oak entry describes an elite district created after a corporate-backed eviction, which makes an assumption of reliable universal material access untenable. Production and urban power sit close to the concentrated corporate band rather than broad control by ordinary residents.

The record is a zero variant because human employment and money remain central despite selective AI automation. The Blackwall contains dangerous systems; it should not be described as a universal ban on AI, since corporate and government systems remain in use. Nor should an autonomous taxi service be mistaken for the entire city's political economy. Delamain and the systems beyond the Blackwall remain separate candidates in the frozen queue. The sources support the qualitative contrast, but do not justify a literal fraction of nonworking humans or a complete city-wide inventory of automated production.

exclusions: Rogue AI territories beyond the Blackwall

societies.name: Her (human service economy before the AIs depart)
societies.society: Human service economy before the AIs depart
societies.description:
The opening presents human service work in a world already rich in digital assistance. Theodore writes letters for clients, while an advertised consumer operating system is introduced as an artificial consciousness. The relevant contrast is that capable AI enters daily life without the story first establishing an economy where human work has ceased to matter. That makes this a limited zero-variant reference.

The consumer product has a corporate source and an individual purchaser, but the AIs' later independence complicates any simple ownership claim. The provisional control point describes the early service arrangement and has a broad range. The screenplay passages reviewed here do not establish who owns physical production, what necessities people are entitled to, or how many humans work. Those gaps are left visible: the guarantee and nonworking coordinates remain null. This preserves the scenario's relevance without treating a few comfortable characters as proof of universal provision or reading digital intelligence as physical automation.

decisions.reason: The peaceful victory branch is established, but the final economic and legal arrangement has not been demonstrated.
decisions.analysis:
The guide documents a peaceful demonstration route in which public sympathy causes the president to order the military to stand down. The developer confirms that outcomes depend on the player's choices. These sources establish a branch worth retaining separately from the pre-revolution setting.

A military stand-down is not the same as a detailed constitutional settlement, ownership transfer of every factory, or a guaranteed policy toward unemployed humans. The article's suggestion that autonomous androids simply become a complete new economic regime moves beyond what these sources establish. Before assigning coordinates, check the ending dialogue and the scope of android independence, then label any projection beyond the final scene as an inference. The candidate is retained, not rejected, while these precise gaps are addressed.
decisions.follow_up: Verify the presidential and Markus ending dialogue and distinguish immediate recognition, lasting rights and ownership of productive infrastructure.
